<reason>Both sides argued competently and honestly answered pressure with clear A1/A2 labels, but CON made the debate easier to decide. CON tracked PRO's concessions across rounds (developer can publish and ship; real findings travel via confidential submission; challenges stay secret and rotate) and assembled them into a coherent picture of what the regime actually delivers: a completion stamp read as clearance, category-level public statements, and comparability that only the regulator can judge. PRO's core route—mandatory beats voluntary disclosure, and evidence-before-exposure has preventive value—stayed live and was defended reasonably (the timing distinction on reputational costs in the closing was a fair answer, and "nothing exempts liability" blunted the waiver claim). But PRO never fully repaired the comparability problem after CON's "the result is the challenge" point, and its answers increasingly relied on the confidential regulator channel, which fed CON's argument that publication adds little. CON's weak spots (finite-resources tradeoff, "defenders already assume" glibness, admitting liability doesn't force pre-launch disclosure) kept this competitive rather than decisive.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B4.5–B4.7: CON's answer to PRO's comparability question ("the result is the challenge"—scores against secret rotating prompt sets tell outsiders nothing comparable, and protocol versions only help those who see them) followed by the summary of what PRO's answers leave standing. It converted PRO's own clarifications into the case that the public-facing output is an uninformative stamp.</best_rebuttal>
